options: A value that can go up or down, like memory usage
A cumulative metric that only ever increases (or resets on restart)
A fixed configuration value set once at startup
A metric type used only for alerting, never for graphs
questions.explain: A counter is cumulative and only increases — total requests, total errors. It resets to zero only when the process restarts, and is almost always queried with rate() rather than graphed raw.

questions.q: Why do you almost never graph a raw counter value directly?
options: Counters can't be scraped by Prometheus
The raw value is just an ever-climbing staircase that tells you little about the current rate of activity
Counters don't support labels
Graphing counters is a security risk
questions.explain: A raw counter only climbs, so its absolute value (like '12 million requests since start') isn't informative on its own. Applying rate() converts it into a per-second rate that's actually useful.

questions.q: What's the key difference between a gauge and a counter?
options: A gauge can go up and down; a counter only ever increases
A gauge is only for strings, a counter only for numbers
There is no difference — they're interchangeable terms
A gauge requires Alertmanager; a counter does not
questions.explain: A gauge represents a value that can rise and fall, like active sessions or memory usage, and is graphed directly. A counter only ever increases.

questions.q: What does a histogram metric let you calculate that a plain counter or gauge can't?
options: The total number of scrape targets
Latency percentiles, by bucketing observations like request durations
The uptime of the Prometheus server itself
The number of labels on a metric
questions.explain: A histogram samples observations (often durations) into configurable buckets, which lets you calculate percentiles like 'the 95th percentile request took under 0.5 seconds' using histogram_quantile() in PromQL.

questions.q: Why would you choose a histogram over a summary for request duration, if you have multiple instances of a service?
options: Summaries aren't supported by any client library
A histogram's bucketed data can be aggregated across instances; a summary's client-side percentiles cannot
Histograms use less memory than summaries in every case
There's no reason — they produce identical results
questions.explain: A summary calculates percentiles client-side per instance, so you can't meaningfully combine those percentiles across multiple instances. A histogram's bucket counts can be aggregated and then have a percentile calculated server-side with histogram_quantile().
